options.text: Wait for the tools to be automatically discovered

options.label: B
options.text: Restart Claude Code to re-establish MCP connections

options.label: C
options.text: Restart Claude Code to trigger tool rediscovery

options.label: D
options.text: Manually refresh the tool cache in Claude Code

explanation: Tools are discovered during connection establishment. After server updates, Claude Code needs to restart to establish new connections and discover updated tools.

stem: Your document analysis agent needs to process 50,000 research papers. Agents currently struggle to find relevant documents efficiently. How should you restructure the MCP integration?

options.label: A
options.text: Create individual tools for each document category

options.label: B
options.text: Implement MCP resources with hierarchical browsing of the document catalog

options.label: C
options.text: Use prompts to describe document locations and metadata

options.label: D
options.text: Build a single search tool that returns all matching documents

explanation: MCP resources provide the appropriate interface for large content catalogs, allowing agents to browse and discover documents hierarchically rather than relying on search tools alone.

stem: Your support system needs CRM integration, email sending, and timezone conversion. Development resources are limited. What is the most pragmatic server architecture?

options.label: A
options.text: Build one custom MCP server containing all three capabilities

options.label: B
options.text: Use community servers for email and timezone, build custom CRM integration

options.label: C
options.text: Build separate custom MCP servers for each capability

options.label: D
options.text: Use only community servers and modify them for CRM integration

explanation: With limited resources, leveraging community servers for standard functionality (email, timezone) while building custom integration only for proprietary systems (CRM) maximizes efficiency.

stem: Your research team wants to test different web search MCP servers (Brave, DuckDuckGo, Google) for performance comparison. How should you structure the configuration?

options.label: A
options.text: Configure all three servers in the project .mcp.json

options.label: B
options.text: Have each team member test different servers using their ~/.claude.json

options.label: C
options.text: Create separate branches for each search server configuration

options.label: D
options.text: Use environment variables to switch between servers dynamically

explanation: User-level ~/.claude.json configuration allows team members to test different MCP servers independently without affecting shared project configuration or requiring code changes.

stem: Your support system's MCP configuration needs different database credentials for development, staging, and production. Your current config hard-codes production credentials. What changes should you make?

options.label: A
options.text: Create separate .mcp.json files for each environment

options.label: B
options.text: Replace hard-coded credentials with ${DB_USER} and ${DB_PASS} environment variables

options.label: C
options.text: Use conditional logic in the .mcp.json file

options.label: D
options.text: Store credentials in a separate configuration service

explanation: Environment variable expansion with ${VAR} syntax allows the same .mcp.json to work across environments while keeping credentials secure and environment-specific.

stem: Your research system's MCP server dynamically generates tools based on available data sources. After adding new research databases, agents don't see the new tools. When will they become available?

options.label: A
options.text: Immediately when the databases are added

options.label: B
options.text: When the next agent request is processed

options.label: C
options.text: When Claude Code reconnects to the MCP server

options.label: D
options.text: After manually triggering tool refresh

explanation: Tool discovery occurs during connection establishment. Even for dynamically generated tools, Claude Code must reconnect to the MCP server to discover newly available tools.

stem: Your support agents need access to a knowledge base with 10,000 FAQ articles, product documentation, and policy documents. Currently using individual search tools for each category results in poor discoverability. What MCP approach would improve this?

options.label: A
options.text: Combine all search tools into a single unified search tool

options.label: B
options.text: Implement MCP resources to expose the knowledge base structure for browsing

options.label: C
options.text: Create more granular search tools for subcategories

options.label: D
options.text: Use MCP prompts to provide search guidance

explanation: MCP resources provide a browsable interface for large content catalogs, allowing agents to explore and discover relevant information more effectively than search-only approaches.

stem: Your research system needs PDF processing, web scraping, and proprietary academic database access. The academic database has a unique authentication scheme. What server strategy minimizes development time while ensuring reliability?

options.label: A
options.text: Build all three capabilities in a single custom MCP server for consistency

options.label: B
options.text: Use community servers for PDF and web scraping, build custom server for academic database

options.label: C
options.text: Use community servers for all capabilities and modify them for the database

options.label: D
options.text: Build separate custom servers for each capability for maximum control

explanation: Leveraging proven community servers for standard functionality (PDF, web scraping) while building custom integration only for proprietary systems minimizes development time and leverages community maintenance.

stem: A developer accidentally committed their personal API keys in the project .mcp.json file. Beyond removing the keys, what configuration change prevents this in the future?

options.label: A
options.text: Move all MCP configuration to individual ~/.claude.json files

options.label: B
options.text: Replace hard-coded keys with environment variable references like ${API_KEY}

options.label: C
options.text: Add .mcp.json to .gitignore

options.label: D
options.text: Use a separate configuration file for sensitive values

explanation: Using environment variable expansion prevents credentials from being committed to version control while maintaining shared project configuration structure.

stem: Your research system's MCP server fails to authenticate with external APIs in your containerized deployment. The .mcp.json uses "token": "${RESEARCH_TOKEN}". Container logs show the MCP server starting successfully. What is the most likely issue?

options.label: A
options.text: The container doesn't have network access to the external APIs

options.label: B
options.text: The RESEARCH_TOKEN environment variable is not set in the container

options.label: C
options.text: The MCP server doesn't support environment variable expansion

options.label: D
options.text: The external API endpoints are different in the container environment

explanation: In containerized deployments, environment variables must be explicitly passed to containers. If ${RESEARCH_TOKEN} isn't set, the literal string is used instead of the token value.

stem: Your billing MCP server implements conditional tool availability based on user permissions. Support agents with different roles see different tools. A new agent reports seeing no tools despite proper permissions. What should you check first?

options.label: A
options.text: Whether the agent's permissions are correctly configured in the billing system

options.label: B
options.text: Whether Claude Code successfully connected to the MCP server for this agent

options.label: C
options.text: Whether the MCP server is implementing tools/list correctly for this user

options.label: D
options.text: Whether the agent is using the correct .mcp.json configuration

explanation: If no tools are visible, the first step is verifying connection establishment. Tool discovery happens during connection, so connection failure would result in no tools being available regardless of permissions.

stem: Your document analysis agents are making excessive API calls because they can't efficiently browse your research paper collection. Each search query hits the database multiple times. How should you optimize the MCP integration?

options.label: A
options.text: Implement caching in the search tools

options.label: B
options.text: Expose the paper catalog structure through MCP resources

options.label: C
options.text: Reduce the number of available search tools

options.label: D
options.text: Implement batch search capabilities

explanation: MCP resources allow agents to browse and understand the structure of content catalogs without repeated API calls, reducing database load and improving agent efficiency.

stem: Your support system needs Slack integration, calendar scheduling, and access to your proprietary customer database. A community Slack MCP server exists but lacks some features you need. What approach balances functionality and maintenance burden?

options.label: A
options.text: Fork and modify the community Slack server, build custom servers for calendar and database

options.label: B
options.text: Build all three as custom MCP servers for consistency

options.label: C
options.text: Use the community Slack server as-is and build custom servers for missing functionality

options.label: D
options.text: Build one comprehensive custom server containing all three integrations

explanation: Forking the community server allows customization while maintaining community updates as a base. Building separate custom servers for other proprietary systems provides modularity and focused functionality.

stem: Your research team wants to standardize on specific MCP servers but allow individual researchers to add experimental servers for their specific projects. How should you structure the configuration?

options.label: A
options.text: Put all servers in project .mcp.json and use feature flags

options.label: B
options.text: Use project .mcp.json for standard servers, allow additional servers in ~/.claude.json

options.label: C
options.text: Use only ~/.claude.json files with shared templates

options.label: D
options.text: Create separate project configurations for each researcher

explanation: Project-level .mcp.json ensures consistent core functionality while user-level ~/.claude.json allows individual experimentation without affecting team standards or requiring project changes.

stem: Your customer support MCP configuration needs to work across multiple deployment environments with different database hosts and credentials. Currently each environment requires manual configuration file changes. What solution provides the most maintainable approach?

options.label: A
options.text: Create separate .mcp.json files for each environment

options.label: B
options.text: Use environment variables like ${DB_HOST} and ${DB_CREDENTIALS} in a single .mcp.json

options.label: C
options.text: Use a configuration management tool to template the .mcp.json

options.label: D
options.text: Implement runtime configuration loading in the MCP server

explanation: Environment variable expansion allows a single configuration file to work across all environments by substituting environment-specific values at runtime, reducing maintenance overhead.

stem: A developer implements an MCP server that dynamically adds tools based on runtime conditions. They add logic to check for new tools every 30 seconds during agent conversations. What is the primary flaw in this approach?

options.label: A
options.text: The polling interval is too frequent and will impact performance

options.label: B
options.text: MCP tools are discovered only during connection establishment, not during runtime

options.label: C
options.text: Dynamic tool addition requires restart of the MCP server

options.label: D
options.text: Runtime tool checking should be event-driven rather than polling-based

explanation: This is a fundamental misunderstanding of MCP tool discovery. Tools are discovered during the connection handshake phase, not continuously during runtime. Runtime polling won't make new tools available.

stem: A team lead decides to avoid project-level .mcp.json configuration entirely, instead providing each team member with identical ~/.claude.json files to ensure consistency. What is the main problem with this approach?

options.label: A
options.text: User-level configuration files cannot be version controlled effectively

options.label: B
options.text: Individual ~/.claude.json files have limited MCP server capacity

options.label: C
options.text: User-level configuration requires more system resources

options.label: D
options.text: Multiple ~/.claude.json files create connection conflicts

explanation: User-level configurations are outside version control, making it impossible to track changes, ensure consistency, or manage updates across team members. Project-level configuration should be used for shared resources.

stem: A developer creates an MCP server that reads .mcp.json at runtime and performs its own environment variable substitution using custom parsing logic like %VAR% and {{VAR}}. What is the fundamental issue with this approach?

options.label: A
options.text: Custom parsing logic introduces unnecessary complexity and potential bugs

options.label: B
options.text: MCP clients handle environment variable expansion using ${VAR} syntax, making server-side parsing redundant

options.label: C
options.text: Multiple variable syntax formats create confusion for developers

options.label: D
options.text: Runtime configuration parsing impacts MCP server performance

explanation: Environment variable expansion is handled by the MCP client (Claude Code) using standard ${VAR} syntax. Server-side parsing duplicates this functionality and ignores the standard MCP configuration mechanism.

stem: A developer builds a customer knowledge base MCP server that implements 500+ individual tools, one for each FAQ category and subcategory, believing this provides the most specific access. What is the primary problem with this approach?

options.label: A
options.text: Too many tools create overwhelming choice paralysis for agents

options.label: B
options.text: MCP resources would provide a more appropriate interface for browsing content catalogs

options.label: C
options.text: Individual tools have higher latency than batch operations

options.label: D
options.text: Large numbers of tools exceed MCP server connection limits

explanation: This over-engineers the solution by creating tools for what should be resources. MCP resources are specifically designed for content catalogs and browsable data structures, not individual tools.

stem: A team decides to build custom MCP servers for all functionality including basic operations like file system access, web requests, and JSON parsing, believing custom implementation provides better control. What is the key flaw in this strategy?

options.label: A
options.text: Custom servers require more computational resources than community servers

options.label: B
options.text: This unnecessarily duplicates well-tested community functionality and increases maintenance burden

options.label: C
options.text: Custom servers cannot integrate with community MCP ecosystems

options.label: D
options.text: Multiple custom servers create version compatibility issues

explanation: This represents over-engineering by building custom solutions for standard functionality. Community servers provide tested implementations with ongoing maintenance, while custom servers for basic operations add unnecessary development and maintenance overhead.

stem: A developer implements error handling in their support agent that catches 'tool not found' errors and attempts to trigger MCP server reconnection to refresh available tools. What misconception does this approach reflect?

options.label: A
options.text: Tool availability should be verified before each tool call rather than handling errors

options.label: B
options.text: MCP connections should be persistent and not reconnected for tool discovery

options.label: C
options.text: Tool discovery happens at connection time, so missing tools indicate connection issues, not discovery timing

options.label: D
options.text: Error handling should be implemented at the MCP server level, not the agent level

explanation: This reflects a misunderstanding that tools can appear/disappear during runtime. If a tool is 'not found', it indicates either the tool was never discovered (connection issue) or the tool name is incorrect, not a timing issue requiring reconnection.

stem: A developer creates a complex system where the project .mcp.json dynamically generates different configurations based on the current user's ~/.claude.json settings, believing this provides the best of both approaches. What is the primary issue with this design?

options.label: A
options.text: Dynamic configuration generation creates unpredictable behavior and debugging difficulties

options.label: B
options.text: User-level settings should not influence project-level configuration

options.label: C
options.text: This approach requires elevated file system permissions

options.label: D
options.text: Cross-file configuration dependencies impact MCP server performance

explanation: This over-complicates the configuration system by creating interdependencies between user and project configurations. It makes debugging difficult and behavior unpredictable, violating the principle of clear separation between user and project settings.

stem: Your customer support agent needs to search through log files to find all instances of a specific customer ID across multiple files. Which built-in tool is most appropriate for this content search task?

options.label: A
options.text: Read tool to sequentially examine each file

options.label: B
options.text: Glob tool to match files containing the customer ID

options.label: C
options.text: Grep tool to search for the customer ID pattern across files

options.label: D
options.text: Edit tool to locate and highlight matching content

explanation: Grep is specifically designed for content search across files, making it the optimal choice for finding customer ID instances. Read would be inefficient for searching, Glob matches file paths not content, and Edit is for modifications not search.

stem: Your document analysis agent needs to process all PDF research papers in a directory structure that follows the pattern '/research/papers/2024/*.pdf'. Which tool should it use to identify these files?

options.label: A
options.text: Grep tool to search for '.pdf' in file contents

options.label: B
options.text: Read tool to check each file's extension

options.label: C
options.text: Edit tool to locate PDF files

options.label: D
options.text: Glob tool to match the file path pattern

explanation: Glob is designed for file path pattern matching and can efficiently find all files matching '/research/papers/2024/*.pdf'. Grep searches content not paths, Read requires knowing specific filenames, and Edit is for modifications.

stem: Your support agent needs to create a complete incident report file from scratch with customer details, timestamps, and resolution steps. Which approach uses the appropriate built-in tool?

options.label: A
options.text: Write tool to create the complete file with all content

options.label: B
options.text: Edit tool to create and populate the new file

options.label: C
options.text: Grep tool to template the report structure

options.label: D
options.text: Glob tool to generate the file from a pattern

explanation: Write tool is designed for full file operations including creating new files with complete content. Edit requires existing content to modify, Grep is for searching, and Glob is for path matching.

key_concept_tested: Edit: targeted modifications with unique text matching
stem: Your report generation agent needs to update a specific section in an existing research report by replacing the text 'Preliminary findings suggest' with 'Comprehensive analysis confirms'. Which tool is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Grep tool to find and replace the text

options.label: B
options.text: Edit tool to make the targeted text replacement

options.label: C
options.text: Write tool to recreate the entire file

options.label: D
options.text: Read tool to locate the text for manual replacement

explanation: Edit tool is designed for targeted modifications using unique text matching, perfect for replacing specific phrases. Grep only searches, Write would require recreating the entire file, and Read doesn't perform modifications.

stem: Your support agent attempts to use Edit tool to update a customer configuration file, but the operation fails because the target text pattern appears multiple times. What is the most reliable fallback approach?

options.label: A
options.text: Retry Edit with a more specific pattern

options.label: B
options.text: Use Grep to find all instances then Edit each one

options.label: C
options.text: Use Read to get full content, modify it, then Write the complete file

options.label: D
options.text: Use Glob to find similar files and Edit them instead

explanation: When Edit fails due to ambiguous patterns, the standard fallback is Read + Write: read the full file, make modifications to the content, then write the complete updated file. This ensures precise control over all changes.

stem: Your document analysis agent needs to understand a large research codebase structure before processing files. The codebase has 500+ files across multiple directories. What is the most efficient approach to build understanding incrementally?

options.label: A
options.text: Use Read on all files to get complete understanding

options.label: B
options.text: Start with Glob to map structure, then Grep key terms, then Read specific files

options.label: C
options.text: Use Grep to search for main functions across all files

options.label: D
options.text: Use Glob for directory structure, Read key files like README/main, then targeted Grep/Read

explanation: Incremental understanding follows: Glob for structure overview, Read key entry points (README, main files), then targeted Grep/Read for specific areas. This builds context efficiently without overwhelming the agent with all files upfront.

stem: Your customer support agent needs to find all error messages containing 'payment_failed' across log files from the past week to identify patterns. The logs are in /var/logs/app-*.log format. Which approach is most efficient?

options.label: A
options.text: Use Grep with 'payment_failed' pattern across the log directory

options.label: B
options.text: Use Glob to find log files, then Read each one to search manually

options.label: C
options.text: Use Read on each log file and manually scan for the error

options.label: D
options.text: Use Edit to highlight all instances of 'payment_failed'

explanation: Grep is designed for efficient content search across multiple files and can search for 'payment_failed' across all matching log files in one operation. Other approaches are inefficient or inappropriate for search tasks.

stem: Your research system needs to process academic papers from multiple years and formats. The files are organized as '/research/2023/papers/*.pdf', '/research/2024/papers/*.pdf', and '/research/2024/drafts/*.docx'. How should you efficiently identify all relevant documents?

options.label: A
options.text: Use three separate Read operations for each directory

options.label: B
options.text: Use multiple Glob patterns: '/research/*/papers/*.pdf' and '/research/2024/drafts/*.docx'

options.label: C
options.text: Use Grep to search for file extensions across the research directory

options.label: D
options.text: Use Edit to list all files in the research directory

explanation: Multiple Glob patterns efficiently match the different directory structures and file types. The wildcard patterns capture the year variations and different file locations without needing to know specific filenames.

stem: Your support agent needs to generate a comprehensive customer history report by combining data from multiple sources: account info, transaction logs, and support tickets. The final report will be 2000+ lines. What's the most appropriate approach?

options.label: A
options.text: Use Edit to incrementally build the report section by section

options.label: B
options.text: Use Grep to extract relevant data and combine manually

options.label: C
options.text: Use Read to gather all source data, then Write the complete report

options.label: D
options.text: Use Glob to template the report structure

explanation: For large, comprehensive reports combining multiple data sources, the Read + Write pattern is most appropriate: Read source data, process and combine it, then Write the complete report. Edit is not suitable for building large files from scratch.

key_concept_tested: Edit: targeted modifications with unique text matching
stem: Your synthesis agent needs to update citation numbers in a research report after adding new references. The report contains '[1]', '[2]', '[3]' etc., and you need to increment all numbers by 5. What's the most reliable approach?

options.label: A
options.text: Use multiple Edit operations to replace each citation individually

options.label: B
options.text: Use Grep to find all citations then Edit each pattern

options.label: C
options.text: Use Glob to match citation patterns

options.label: D
options.text: Use Read + Write to process all citations programmatically

explanation: When making systematic changes to multiple similar patterns, Read + Write is more reliable than multiple Edit operations. This allows programmatic processing of all citation numbers in one operation, avoiding potential Edit failures with similar patterns.

stem: Your support agent needs to understand a customer's custom integration codebase to debug their API connection issues. The codebase is unfamiliar and contains 200+ files. How should the agent approach this systematically?

options.label: A
options.text: Use Read on every file to get complete understanding

options.label: B
options.text: Use Grep to search for 'API' across all files immediately

options.label: C
options.text: Use Glob for structure, Read entry points, then Grep for API-related code

options.label: D
options.text: Use Edit to add debugging statements throughout the codebase

explanation: For debugging specific issues, starting with structural understanding (Glob), then reading key files (README, main entry points), then targeted searches (Grep for 'API', 'connection', error handling) is most efficient. Reading all files first would be overwhelming and inefficient.

stem: Your document analysis agent is processing research papers and needs to identify all papers that cite a specific author 'Johnson, M.' across a collection of 500+ PDF text files. Performance is critical as this runs frequently. What's the optimal approach?

options.label: A
options.text: Use Read on each file and manually search for the author name

options.label: B
options.text: Use Grep to search for 'Johnson, M.' across all text files

options.label: C
options.text: Use Glob to find files with 'Johnson' in the filename

options.label: D
options.text: Use Edit to highlight author citations in each file

explanation: Grep is optimized for content search across multiple files and will efficiently find all instances of 'Johnson, M.' across the entire collection. This is much faster than reading each file individually and more appropriate than filename matching or editing operations.

stem: Your customer support system stores escalation records in files following the pattern '/escalations/2024/month-XX/case-XXXXX.json' where XX is the month and XXXXX is the case number. You need to find all escalations from Q4 2024 (months 10-12). What's the most efficient Glob pattern approach?

options.label: A
options.text: Use three separate Glob patterns for each month: month-10, month-11, month-12

options.label: B
options.text: Use pattern '/escalations/2024/month-1[0-2]/*.json' to match months 10-12

options.label: C
options.text: Use Grep to search for '10', '11', '12' in file paths

options.label: D
options.text: Use Read to check each directory individually

explanation: The pattern '/escalations/2024/month-1[0-2]/*.json' efficiently matches months 10, 11, and 12 using character class notation. This is more efficient than multiple separate patterns and more precise than searching content or reading directories.

key_concept_tested: Edit: targeted modifications with unique text matching
stem: Your report generation agent needs to update the status of multiple research projects in a summary file. Each project has a unique ID and status line like 'Project Alpha-2024-001: In Progress'. You need to change specific projects to 'Completed'. What's the safest approach?

options.label: A
options.text: Use Edit with the full unique line as the target pattern

options.label: B
options.text: Use Grep to find the lines then Edit with project ID

options.label: C
options.text: Use multiple Edit operations with just the status text

options.label: D
options.text: Use Edit with the unique project ID as the target pattern

explanation: Using the unique project ID as the target pattern ensures Edit can reliably identify and modify the correct line. Using the full line or just status text could cause issues if patterns are similar, while using the unique ID provides precise targeting.

stem: Your support agent is trying to update a customer configuration file using Edit, but the operation fails with an error indicating the target text 'timeout: 30' appears in 15 different locations. The agent needs to update only the database timeout setting. What should it do next?

options.label: A
options.text: Try Edit again with a more specific pattern like 'database timeout: 30'

options.label: B
options.text: Use Read to get the full file, locate the correct setting, then Write the updated file

options.label: C
options.text: Use Grep to find all timeout settings then manually choose which to edit

options.label: D
options.text: Use Glob to find similar configuration files to compare

explanation: When Edit fails due to multiple matches, the first approach should be using a more specific unique pattern. If that still fails, then fall back to Read + Write. The more specific pattern 'database timeout: 30' is likely to be unique.

stem: Your document analysis agent encounters a complex research codebase with machine learning models. It needs to understand the data preprocessing pipeline to process similar documents. The codebase has 300+ Python files. What's the most systematic approach?

options.label: A
options.text: Use Grep to search for 'preprocess' across all files immediately

options.label: B
options.text: Use Glob for structure, Read main.py and README, then Grep for preprocessing terms

options.label: C
options.text: Use Read on all Python files to understand everything

options.label: D
options.text: Use Edit to add logging to trace the preprocessing flow

explanation: Incremental understanding starts with structure (Glob), then key entry points (main.py, README), then targeted searches for specific functionality (Grep for 'preprocess', 'pipeline', 'transform'). This builds context systematically without information overload.

stem: A junior developer suggests using Read tool to search for customer complaint patterns across 500+ support ticket files by reading each file sequentially and manually scanning the content. What is the primary flaw in this approach?

options.label: A
options.text: Read tool cannot handle large numbers of files

options.label: B
options.text: Sequential reading is too slow and inefficient compared to Grep's optimized search

options.label: C
options.text: Grep tool is specifically designed for content search across multiple files

options.label: D
options.text: Manual scanning will miss patterns that automated tools would catch

explanation: The fundamental flaw is using the wrong tool for the job. Grep is specifically designed for efficient content search across multiple files, while Read is for retrieving full file contents. Using Read for search is both inefficient and architecturally incorrect.

stem: A team member proposes using Grep to find all Python files in a research project by searching for '.py' across the entire directory structure. Why is this approach problematic?

options.label: A
options.text: Grep searches file content, not file paths, and will find '.py' in comments and strings

options.label: B
options.text: Glob is designed for file path pattern matching and would be more efficient

options.label: C
options.text: The search pattern '.py' is too broad and will match unrelated content

options.label: D
options.text: Grep requires knowing specific file contents beforehand

explanation: The main issue is using Grep for file path matching when Glob is specifically designed for this purpose. Grep searches file contents and would indeed find '.py' in code comments, strings, and content, not just filenames. Glob with '*.py' pattern is the correct approach.

key_concept_tested: Edit: targeted modifications with unique text matching
stem: A developer suggests using Edit tool to replace all instances of 'error' with 'warning' in log files, arguing it's faster than Read + Write. What is the critical risk with this approach?

options.label: A
options.text: Edit tool is slower than Read + Write for bulk operations

options.label: B
options.text: Edit requires unique text patterns and 'error' likely appears in many contexts

options.label: C
options.text: Log files should not be modified as they are historical records

options.label: D
options.text: Edit tool cannot handle large files efficiently

explanation: The critical flaw is modifying log files, which are historical records that should remain immutable for audit and debugging purposes. Additionally, 'error' appearing in many contexts would cause Edit to fail due to non-unique patterns, but the primary issue is the inappropriate modification of logs.

stem: A colleague proposes using multiple Edit operations to build a new research report from scratch, adding one section at a time. What is the fundamental problem with this approach?

options.label: A
options.text: Multiple Edit operations will create file locking issues

options.label: B
options.text: Edit requires existing content to modify; it's not designed for creating new files

options.label: C
options.text: Write tool would be more efficient for incremental additions

options.label: D
options.text: Edit operations are not atomic and could corrupt the file

explanation: Edit tool requires existing content to modify and unique text patterns to target. It's not designed for creating files from scratch. Write tool is the appropriate choice for creating new files with complete content.

stem: A new team member suggests immediately using Grep to search for specific error handling patterns across an unfamiliar customer codebase without any prior exploration. What is the main risk of this approach?

options.label: A
options.text: Grep searches will be too slow without indexing the codebase first

options.label: B
options.text: Without understanding the codebase structure, searches may miss relevant code or return overwhelming results

options.label: C
options.text: The agent lacks context to interpret search results meaningfully

options.label: D
options.text: Error handling patterns vary too much to search effectively

explanation: Jumping directly to targeted searches without building contextual understanding first means the agent cannot meaningfully interpret the results. Incremental understanding (structure → key files → targeted searches) provides necessary context to make search results actionable.

stem: When an Edit operation fails due to ambiguous patterns, a developer suggests trying the same Edit command multiple times with slight variations rather than using Read + Write. What is wrong with this approach?

options.label: A
options.text: Multiple Edit attempts will cause file corruption

options.label: B
options.text: Edit variations are still probabilistic; Read + Write provides deterministic control

options.label: C

stem: Your customer support agent needs to read the complete contents of a customer's configuration file to analyze their current settings. Which built-in tool is designed for this full file retrieval operation?

stem: Your report generation agent needs to update a single date field in a research report from '2024-01-15' to '2024-01-20'. The date appears only once in the document. Which tool is most appropriate for this targeted modification?

stem: Your support system stores customer data files with names like 'customer-12345.json', 'customer-67890.json' in the /data directory. Which tool should you use to find all customer data files?

stem: When an Edit operation fails because the target text pattern is not unique enough, what is the standard fallback approach?

stem: When approaching an unfamiliar codebase for the first time, what is the recommended first step in the incremental understanding pattern?

stem: Your customer support agent needs to analyze escalation patterns by finding all instances where customers mentioned 'frustrated', 'angry', or 'disappointed' across 1000+ support chat transcripts. The analysis runs daily and performance matters. What's the optimal approach?

stem: Your synthesis agent needs to merge findings from 5 different research subagents into a final comprehensive report. Each subagent provides a detailed section (200-500 lines each). stem: Your support agent needs to understand how a customer's payment processing integration works to debug a recurring billing issue. The integration codebase has 150 files including config files, API handlers, database models, and tests. What's the most systematic debugging approach?

stem: Your report generation agent attempts to update research status indicators throughout a 50-page document using Edit. stem: Your team wants to establish consistent coding standards across all Claude Code sessions for every developer. Where should you place the CLAUDE.md file to ensure these standards apply globally for each team member?

stem: Your React application has distinct frontend and backend API modules with different coding conventions. stem: A developer suggests this CLAUDE.md structure for a large codebase: 'Just copy-paste all our coding standards, API documentation, and testing guidelines directly into each CLAUDE.md file to ensure Claude has complete context.' What is the primary flaw with this approach?

explanation: While duplication and maintenance overhead are concerns, the primary technical flaw is that excessively large CLAUDE.md files can exceed context limits and reduce Claude's effectiveness. The @import syntax allows modular organization while keeping individual files focused and within optimal size limits.

stem: Your team has established coding standards for security (authentication patterns, input validation), performance (caching strategies, database queries), and accessibility (ARIA labels, keyboard navigation). options.label: D

stem: After configuring multiple CLAUDE.md files across your project hierarchy, you want to verify that Claude Code is correctly loading and applying the configuration. Which command should you use?

stem: Your microservices project has 8 services, each with unique database schemas, API patterns, and testing frameworks. The services share common Docker configurations and CI/CD patterns. How should you structure CLAUDE.md files for optimal context without duplication?

stem: A team lead proposes: 'Let's put everyone's personal coding preferences (indentation style, bracket placement, variable naming) in the project's .claude/CLAUDE.md so the whole team stays consistent.' What's wrong with this approach?

stem: Your organization maintains shared coding standards in a separate repository (coding-standards.git) that multiple teams reference. You want your project's CLAUDE.md to include these standards without copying them. What's the correct approach?

stem: You have CLAUDE.md files at ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md (user-level), ./CLAUDE.md (project root), and src/api/CLAUDE.md (directory-level). When working in the src/api/ directory, which configuration takes precedence?

stem: A developer writes this in their CLAUDE.md: '@import https://raw.githubusercontent.com/company/standards/main/coding-rules.md' and expects it to pull the latest coding standards from GitHub. Why won't this work?

stem: Your monorepo contains 3 Next.js applications and 2 Node.js APIs, each in separate packages/ subdirectories. All projects share common ESLint rules and Docker patterns, but have different database and deployment configurations. How should you structure CLAUDE.md files?

stem: When organizing rules in the .claude/rules/ directory, what's the recommended approach for naming and structuring rule files?

stem: Your project has .claude/rules/ files for frontend-patterns.md, backend-patterns.md, mobile-patterns.md, and devops-patterns.md. Different developers work on different parts of the system. How should individual CLAUDE.md files handle imports?

stem: A team places their CLAUDE.md file in the .git/ directory, reasoning: 'This way it's version controlled but won't clutter the project root.' What's wrong with this approach?

stem: After implementing a complex CLAUDE.md hierarchy with multiple @import statements, you want to ensure the configuration is working correctly across different project areas. What's the most systematic approach to validate your setup?

options.text: Archive the current configuration and start fresh with current best practices

options.label: B
options.text: Establish regular configuration review cycles and consolidate/update rules systematically

options.label: C
options.text: Lock the configuration files and require approval for any changes

options.label: D
options.text: Split the configuration by team ownership with each team maintaining their sections

explanation: Configuration maintenance requires ongoing attention. Regular review cycles allow teams to consolidate outdated rules, update practices, and maintain consistency while preserving valuable accumulated knowledge.

key_concept_tested: appropriate content for different CLAUDE.md hierarchy levels
stem: Which of these belongs in a directory-level CLAUDE.md file rather than project-level or user-level configuration?

options.label: A
options.text: Personal keyboard shortcuts and editor preferences

options.label: B
options.text: Company-wide security and compliance requirements

options.label: C
options.text: Module-specific API patterns and data transformation logic

options.label: D
options.text: General TypeScript configuration and linting rules

explanation: Directory-level CLAUDE.md files should contain context-specific guidance that applies to that particular module or component area, such as specific API patterns, data models, or architectural decisions unique to that part of the codebase.

stem: Your team has different roles: frontend developers, backend developers, and DevOps engineers. Each role needs different subsets of your .claude/rules/ files. How should you structure @import statements to optimize Claude's context for each role?

options.label: A
options.text: Create role-specific CLAUDE.md files that @import only relevant rule files for each role

options.label: B
options.text: Use a single CLAUDE.md that imports all rules, relying on Claude to ignore irrelevant ones

options.label: C
options.text: Create separate project directories for each role with independent rule sets

options.label: D
options.text: Use user-level ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md files customized for each role

explanation: Role-specific CLAUDE.md files (or directory-level files in role-specific areas) that selectively @import relevant rules provide focused context without overwhelming Claude with irrelevant information for each developer's workflow.

key_concept_tested: over-reliance on /memory command instead of proper configuration
stem: A developer notices Claude isn't following their coding standards, so they start each session by running /memory and manually typing in the rules they want Claude to follow. What's the fundamental problem with this approach?

options.label: A
options.text: It's inefficient and doesn't persist across sessions, defeating the purpose of CLAUDE.md configuration

options.label: B
options.text: The /memory command is only for debugging, not for providing instructions to Claude

options.label: C
options.text: Manual instructions through /memory override CLAUDE.md files and create conflicts

options.label: D
options.text: It violates team consistency by allowing individual developers to override project standards

explanation: Using /memory to manually provide rules each session is inefficient and doesn't persist. The proper solution is to fix the CLAUDE.md configuration so rules are automatically loaded. /memory should be used for verification, not as a workaround for configuration issues.

key_concept_tested: balancing shared standards with project flexibility
stem: Your organization wants to enforce certain security and compliance standards across all projects, while allowing individual project teams flexibility in their development practices. How should you structure CLAUDE.md configurations to achieve this balance?

options.label: A
options.text: Mandatory user-level ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md with security rules, optional project-level customization

options.label: B
options.text: Shared .claude/rules/ repository for compliance standards, project-level @import plus custom rules

options.label: C
options.text: Single comprehensive organizational CLAUDE.md template that all projects must copy

options.label: D
options.text: Separate compliance validation tools, keep CLAUDE.md files completely project-specific

explanation: A shared repository of compliance and security rules that projects @import, combined with project-specific CLAUDE.md files for development practices, provides the best balance of organizational standards and team flexibility.

stem: Claude Code seems to be ignoring your project-level CLAUDE.md file. What's the first thing you should check?

options.label: A
options.text: Verify the file is named exactly 'CLAUDE.md' (case-sensitive) and is in the correct location

options.label: B
options.text: Check if there's a syntax error in the @import statements

options.label: C
options.text: Ensure the file has proper read permissions for Claude Code

options.label: D
options.text: Restart Claude Code to force a configuration reload

explanation: The most common issue is incorrect file naming or placement. CLAUDE.md must be exactly named (case-sensitive) and in a recognized location (project root or .claude/ directory) for Claude Code to load it.

stem: Your application has different deployment environments (development, staging, production) with different configuration requirements, database connections, and API endpoints. How should CLAUDE.md files handle environment-specific guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: Create separate CLAUDE.md files for each environment in different directories

options.label: B
options.text: Use conditional logic within CLAUDE.md based on environment variables

options.label: C
options.text: Focus CLAUDE.md on code patterns and architecture, keep environment configs in separate files

options.label: D
options.text: Create .claude/rules/ files for each environment and @import based on current context

explanation: CLAUDE.md should focus on code patterns, architecture decisions, and development practices that are consistent across environments. Environment-specific configurations belong in separate config files, not in CLAUDE.md.

stem: A developer writes '@import ../shared-rules/api.md' in their project's CLAUDE.md, expecting to reference a file in a sibling directory. The import fails. What's the likely cause?

options.label: A
options.text: @import paths must be relative to the CLAUDE.md file's location, and the referenced file doesn't exist

options.label: B
options.text: @import doesn't support parent directory references using '../' syntax

options.label: C
options.text: The shared-rules directory needs to be inside the .claude/ folder to be importable

options.label: D
options.text: @import requires absolute paths, not relative paths

explanation: @import paths are resolved relative to the CLAUDE.md file's location. If '../shared-rules/api.md' fails, the most likely cause is that the file doesn't exist at that relative path from the CLAUDE.md file's location.

stem: Your team's CLAUDE.md configuration has become critical to development velocity, but changes sometimes break existing workflows. Multiple developers need to contribute updates. What's the best approach for managing configuration changes?

options.label: A
options.text: Treat CLAUDE.md files like code: use pull requests, reviews, and testing before merging changes

options.label: B
options.text: Designate one senior developer as the configuration owner with exclusive edit rights

options.label: C
options.text: Create a staging branch for configuration changes and merge weekly

options.label: D
options.text: Use separate CLAUDE.md files for each developer to avoid conflicts

explanation: CLAUDE.md files are critical infrastructure that should be managed like code: version controlled, peer reviewed, and tested before deployment. This ensures changes don't break existing workflows while allowing collaborative improvement.

stem: Your team wants to standardize a custom `/generate-tests` command across all developers working on your React project. Where should you place the command file to ensure it's version controlled and available to all team members?

options.label: A
options.text: In ~/.claude/commands/ so each developer can customize it

options.label: B
options.text: In the project root as generate-tests.md

options.label: C
options.text: In .claude/commands/ within the project repository

options.label: D
options.text: In /usr/local/claude/commands/ for system-wide access

explanation: Project-scoped commands belong in .claude/commands/ within the repository. This ensures they're version controlled, shared across the team, and automatically available when working in that project. User-scoped commands (~/.claude/commands/) are for personal commands that shouldn't be shared.

stem: You're building a developer productivity agent that needs to handle 15 different legacy system documentation patterns, each requiring 200+ lines of specific instructions. The agent only uses 2-3 patterns per session. What's the most token-efficient approach?

options.label: A
options.text: Put all patterns in the main CLAUDE.md file for immediate availability

options.label: B
options.text: Create separate skills for each pattern with auto-invocation based on file extensions

options.label: C
options.text: Use a single skill with conditional logic to handle all patterns

options.label: D
options.text: Create individual skills for each pattern, invoked manually via slash commands

explanation: Skills are loaded on-demand, making them more token-efficient than CLAUDE.md for large, infrequently-used instructions. Individual skills allow precise loading of only needed patterns. Auto-invocation could trigger multiple skills unnecessarily, and a single conditional skill would still load all patterns.

stem: A colleague implements a `/code-review` skill that expects to access the current conversation history to understand previous code changes discussed. After deployment, the skill fails to reference earlier context. What's the fundamental issue?

options.label: B
options.text: The skill needs explicit context: fork configuration in frontmatter

options.label: C
options.text: Skills require allowed-tools: ['Read'] to access conversation history

options.label: D
options.text: The skill file is missing the version field in YAML frontmatter

options.label: A
options.text: Skills execute as isolated sub-agents without access to parent conversation context

explanation: Skills execute with fork context, meaning they run as isolated sub-agents without access to the parent conversation history. Any needed context must be explicitly provided in the skill invocation or instructions. The context: fork behavior is intentional for clean skill execution.

stem: You're creating a skill for generating API documentation. Which YAML frontmatter fields are required in your SKILL.md file?

options.label: A
options.text: name, description, allowed-tools

options.label: B
options.text: name, description, version

options.label: C
options.text: name, version, context

options.label: D
options.text: description, version, argument-hint

explanation: The required YAML frontmatter fields for a SKILL.md file are name, description, and version. The name becomes the slash command, description explains the skill's purpose, and version tracks changes. Fields like allowed-tools, context, and argument-hint are optional.

key_concept_tested: allowed-tools frontmatter for skill tool access
stem: Your `/refactor-component` skill needs to read existing files, write modified versions, and run tests to verify changes. Which frontmatter configuration enables these capabilities?

options.label: A
options.text: tools: ["Read", "Write", "Bash"]

options.label: B
options.text: permissions: ["file_read", "file_write", "shell_exec"]

options.label: C
options.text: allowed-tools: ["Read", "Write", "Bash"]

options.label: D
options.text: capabilities: ["Read", "Write", "Bash"]

explanation: The allowed-tools frontmatter field specifies which tools a skill can access. For file operations and test execution, you need Read, Write, and Bash tools. The field name is specifically 'allowed-tools', not 'tools', 'permissions', or 'capabilities'.

stem: A developer puts comprehensive coding standards (500+ lines) directly in CLAUDE.md, claiming "Claude needs this context for every interaction." The team reports slower response times. What's the core problem with this approach?

options.label: A
options.text: CLAUDE.md should only contain project metadata, not detailed instructions

options.label: B
options.text: The standards should be split across multiple CLAUDE.md files in subdirectories

options.label: C
options.text: Large always-loaded context consumes tokens unnecessarily when standards aren't needed

options.label: D
options.text: Coding standards should be implemented as skills, loaded only when relevant

explanation: CLAUDE.md content is always loaded into context, consuming tokens even when not needed. Large instructional content like coding standards should be implemented as skills that load on-demand, improving token efficiency and response times. CLAUDE.md should contain frequently-needed, concise project information.

stem: You're creating a `/migrate-api` skill that requires users to specify the source version, target version, and migration strategy. How should you guide users on the expected input format?

options.label: A
options.text: Include detailed usage examples in the skill description

options.label: B
options.text: Add argument-hint: "source target strategy" to the frontmatter

options.label: C
options.text: Create separate skills for each migration path

options.label: D
options.text: Use input-validation: true in the frontmatter

explanation: The argument-hint frontmatter provides brief parameter guidance, but for complex inputs like API migration parameters, detailed usage examples in the description are more helpful. This gives users clear context on expected formats and options without cluttering the hint field.

stem: Your team uses a custom `/analyze-deps` command that needs to evolve with your project's dependency management practices. What's the primary benefit of placing this in .claude/commands/ versus ~/.claude/commands/?

options.label: A
options.text: Faster execution due to proximity to project files

options.label: B
options.text: Version control integration and team synchronization

options.label: C
options.text: Access to project-specific environment variables

options.label: D
options.text: Automatic activation when entering the project directory

explanation: Project-scoped commands in .claude/commands/ are version controlled with the repository, ensuring all team members have the same command versions and can collaborate on improvements. User-scoped commands (~/.claude/commands/) are personal and not shared or versioned.

key_concept_tested: context fork isolation for skill execution
stem: You're designing a `/security-audit` skill that should analyze code without being influenced by previous conversation context about performance optimizations. Which execution model best serves this requirement?

options.label: A
options.text: Standard execution with full conversation context

options.label: B
options.text: Context: shared to maintain conversation awareness

options.label: C
options.text: Context: fork for isolated, unbiased analysis

options.label: D
options.text: Context: append to build on previous analysis

explanation: Context: fork creates an isolated sub-agent execution environment, perfect for security audits that should be unbiased by previous conversation context. This prevents performance optimization discussions from influencing security analysis, ensuring objective evaluation.

stem: A developer creates skills that auto-invoke based on file extensions: `/analyze-js` for .js files, `/analyze-ts` for .ts files, `/analyze-jsx` for .jsx files. Users report slow responses and irrelevant analysis when browsing code. What's the issue?

options.label: A
options.text: Auto-invocation triggers multiple skills simultaneously, causing context conflicts

options.label: B
options.text: Skills should use manual slash command invocation for precise control

options.label: C
options.text: File extension triggers are too broad, causing unnecessary skill activation

options.label: D
options.text: Auto-invocation loads skills even when users just want to browse, not analyze

explanation: Auto-invocation based on file extensions triggers skills whenever those files are accessed, even for simple browsing. This wastes tokens and provides unwanted analysis. Skills should be invoked intentionally when analysis is actually needed, not automatically on file access.

stem: You have a personal `/my-notes` command for quick note-taking that you don't want to share with your team. Where should this command be placed?

options.label: A
options.text: ~/.claude/commands/ for personal use only

options.label: B
options.text: .claude/commands/ but add it to .gitignore

options.label: C
options.text: .claude/personal/commands/ within the project

options.label: D
options.text: /tmp/claude/commands/ for temporary access

explanation: User-scoped commands belong in ~/.claude/commands/ and are personal to the individual user. They're not version controlled or shared with the team. Project-scoped commands (.claude/commands/) are meant for team collaboration and should be shared.

stem: Your team needs to organize 12 different code analysis skills (linting, security, performance, documentation, etc.). What's the most maintainable directory structure in .claude/skills/?

options.label: A
options.text: One SKILL.md file with all analysis patterns

options.label: B
options.text: Individual directories: lint-analyzer/SKILL.md, security-analyzer/SKILL.md, etc.

options.label: C
options.text: Categorized subdirectories: analysis/lint/SKILL.md, analysis/security/SKILL.md

options.label: D
options.text: Numbered files: 01-lint.md, 02-security.md in .claude/skills/

explanation: Each skill should have its own directory with a SKILL.md file (e.g., lint-analyzer/SKILL.md). This provides clear organization, makes skills easy to find and maintain, and follows the expected directory structure for skill discovery.

stem: A team puts all their development workflows (git conventions, testing patterns, deployment steps, code review checklist) totaling 800 lines in CLAUDE.md, saying "Claude needs to know our full process." What's the efficiency problem?

options.label: A
options.text: CLAUDE.md should be limited to 100 lines maximum

options.label: B
options.text: All content loads into every conversation, wasting tokens when specific workflows aren't needed

options.label: C
options.text: The content should be split into separate CLAUDE.md files per workflow

options.label: D
options.text: Workflow-specific content should be implemented as on-demand skills

explanation: CLAUDE.md content is always loaded, consuming tokens regardless of relevance. Large workflow documentation should be split into skills that load only when needed. This improves token efficiency and response times while maintaining access to detailed process information.

key_concept_tested: skill naming and slash command conventions
stem: You're creating skills for database operations: schema migration, data seeding, backup creation, and query optimization. What naming convention best supports team usability?

options.label: A
options.text: db-migrate, db-seed, db-backup, db-optimize for clear prefixing

options.label: B
options.text: migrate-schema, seed-data, create-backup, optimize-queries for action-first naming

options.label: C
options.text: database-migration, database-seeding, database-backup, database-optimization for full clarity

options.label: D
options.text: migrate, seed, backup, optimize with database context in skill descriptions

explanation: Concise, action-focused names (migrate, seed, backup, optimize) are easier to type and remember. The database context should be clear from the skill descriptions and directory organization. Overly verbose names create friction in daily usage.

key_concept_tested: skill version field purpose and usage
stem: Your `/test-generator` skill has evolved through several iterations with different testing frameworks and patterns. What's the primary purpose of the version field in the YAML frontmatter?

options.label: A
options.text: Enables Claude to automatically update skills to the latest version

options.label: B
options.text: Tracks changes and helps with debugging skill behavior over time

options.label: C
options.text: Determines skill execution priority when multiple versions exist

options.label: D
options.text: Controls compatibility with different Claude model versions

explanation: The version field in skill frontmatter is primarily for tracking changes and helping with maintenance and debugging. It provides a clear history of skill evolution and helps identify which version might have introduced issues or changes in behavior.

key_concept_tested: skill tool requirements and allowed-tools configuration
stem: Your `/deploy-staging` skill needs to read configuration files, execute deployment scripts, search for environment variables in multiple files, and create deployment logs. Which allowed-tools configuration is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: ["Read", "Write", "Bash", "Grep"]

options.label: B
options.text: ["Read", "Bash", "Grep", "Glob"]

options.label: C
options.text: ["Write", "Bash", "Grep", "Glob"]

options.label: D
options.text: ["Read", "Write", "Bash", "Grep", "Glob"]

explanation: The skill needs Read (config files), Write (deployment logs), Bash (deployment scripts), and Grep (searching for environment variables). Glob isn't necessary since the skill can use Read for specific files and Grep for searching within them.

stem: A developer creates a `/fix-bug` skill that references "the error we discussed earlier" and "the previous solution attempt" in its instructions. Users report the skill seems confused and asks for context that was already provided. What's the fundamental misunderstanding?

options.label: A
options.text: The skill needs context: shared instead of the default fork behavior

options.label: B
options.text: Skills execute in isolation and cannot access previous conversation context

options.label: C
options.text: The skill description should include all necessary context instead of referencing conversation history

options.label: D
options.text: Skills require explicit context passing through argument-hint parameters

explanation: Skills execute with fork context (isolation) by default and cannot access previous conversation context. The skill instructions should be self-contained and not reference earlier discussion. Any needed context must be explicitly provided in the skill invocation or built into the instructions.

key_concept_tested: balancing CLAUDE.md vs skills for project context
stem: Your legacy system integration project has: core API patterns (used in 90% of interactions), 8 specialized data transformation patterns (used occasionally), and emergency procedures (rarely needed). How should you organize this information?

options.label: A
options.text: Put everything in CLAUDE.md for comprehensive context

options.label: B
options.text: Core patterns in CLAUDE.md, transformations and procedures as separate skills

options.label: C
options.text: Create skills for all patterns to maximize token efficiency

options.label: D
options.text: Use a single comprehensive skill with all patterns and procedures

explanation: Frequently used core patterns (90% usage) belong in CLAUDE.md for immediate availability. Occasional-use transformations and rare emergency procedures should be skills to avoid token waste. This balances accessibility with efficiency.

key_concept_tested: slash command file naming and discovery
stem: You want to create a `/generate-docs` command for your project. What should be the filename and location for this command?

options.label: A
options.text: .claude/commands/generate-docs.md

options.label: B
options.text: .claude/commands/generate-docs/command.md

options.label: C
options.text: .claude/generate-docs.md

options.label: D
options.text: .claude/commands/generate-docs

explanation: Project-scoped slash commands are placed directly in .claude/commands/ directory with the command name as the filename (generate-docs.md). The filename becomes the slash command name (/generate-docs).

stem: You're creating a `/analyze-performance` skill for identifying bottlenecks in legacy codebases. The skill handles CPU profiling, memory analysis, and database query optimization. What makes for the most effective description?

options.label: A
options.text: "Analyzes code performance"

options.label: B
options.text: "Comprehensive performance analysis including CPU, memory, and database optimization for legacy systems"

options.label: C
options.text: "Performance analyzer - CPU/memory/DB"

options.label: D
options.text: "Identifies performance bottlenecks in code"

explanation: The description should be specific about capabilities (CPU, memory, database) and context (legacy systems) to help users understand when to use the skill. Generic descriptions don't provide enough information for effective skill selection.

stem: A developer creates separate skills for every minor code operation: `/add-import`, `/remove-import`, `/format-function`, `/add-comment`, `/remove-comment`. The team complains about too many slash commands to remember. What's the architectural issue?

options.label: A
options.text: Skills should be grouped by programming language instead of operation type

options.label: B
options.text: Over-granular skills create cognitive overhead without meaningful isolation benefits

options.label: C
options.text: These operations should be combined into broader skills like `/refactor-code` or `/clean-imports`

options.label: D
options.text: Individual operation skills should use auto-invocation instead of manual commands

explanation: Over-granular skills create unnecessary complexity and cognitive load. Related operations should be grouped into cohesive skills (e.g., import management, code formatting) that provide meaningful functionality while remaining discoverable and manageable.

stem: Your `/migrate-database` skill accepts multiple parameters: source database type, target database type, migration strategy (full/incremental), and optional table filters. What's the most helpful argument-hint format?

options.label: A
options.text: "source target strategy [tables]"

options.label: B
options.text: "<source_db> <target_db> <strategy> [table_filter]"

options.label: C
options.text: "database migration parameters"

options.label: D
options.text: "source_database target_database migration_strategy table_filters"

explanation: The argument-hint should use clear parameter names with angle brackets for required parameters and square brackets for optional ones. This format immediately shows users what's required vs optional and provides meaningful parameter names.

stem: You want to create a skill called "api-tester" for testing REST endpoints. What's the correct file structure?

options.label: A
options.text: .claude/skills/api-tester.md

options.label: B
options.text: .claude/skills/api-tester/skill.md

options.label: C
options.text: .claude/skills/api-tester/SKILL.md

options.label: D
options.text: .claude/skills/api-tester/API-TESTER.md

explanation: Skills must be organized in individual directories within .claude/skills/, with the skill definition in a file named SKILL.md (uppercase). The directory name becomes the skill name and slash command.

stem: You're building a `/setup-environment` skill that needs to: check if directories exist, create missing directories, copy template files, modify configuration files, and run initialization scripts. Which tools are essential?

options.label: A
options.text: Read, Write, Bash only

options.label: B
options.text: Read, Write, Bash, Glob

options.label: C
options.text: Write, Bash, Glob only

options.label: D
options.text: Read, Bash, Grep, Glob

explanation: The skill needs Read (check files/configs), Write (create/modify files), Bash (run scripts, create directories), and Glob (find template files). Grep isn't needed for this setup workflow, but Glob is essential for template file discovery.

stem: A team configures their `/security-scan` skill to auto-invoke whenever any .js file is opened, claiming "security should always be checked." Developers report constant unwanted security analysis during normal coding. What's the design flaw?

options.label: A
options.text: Auto-invocation should trigger on file save, not file open

options.label: B
options.text: Security scanning should be a manual process triggered intentionally

options.label: C
options.text: The trigger should be more specific to security-sensitive file patterns

options.label: D
options.text: Auto-invocation should only trigger for modified files, not opened files

explanation: Security scanning is a deliberate analysis activity that shouldn't auto-trigger during normal development workflow. Auto-invocation on file operations creates noise and interrupts the development process. Security scans should be intentionally invoked when needed.

key_concept_tested: personal vs team skill organization strategy
stem: Your team has shared code analysis skills, but you also have personal productivity shortcuts that wouldn't be useful to others. How should you organize these different types of skills?

options.label: A
options.text: All skills in project .claude/skills/ with personal ones marked as such

options.label: B
options.text: Team skills in project .claude/skills/, personal skills in ~/.claude/skills/

options.label: C
options.text: All skills in ~/.claude/skills/ for consistency

options.label: D
options.text: Team skills in project .claude/skills/, personal shortcuts as user-scoped commands in ~/.claude/commands/

explanation: Team-relevant skills belong in the project's .claude/skills/ for version control and sharing. Personal productivity shortcuts are better as user-scoped commands (~/.claude/commands/) since they're simple, personal, and don't need the complexity of skill structure.

stem: You need to create a simple text transformation that converts camelCase to snake_case. This is a straightforward, stateless operation with no tool requirements. What's the most appropriate implementation?

options.label: A
options.text: A skill with detailed transformation logic in SKILL.md

options.label: B
options.text: A slash command with inline transformation instructions

options.label: C
options.text: Include the transformation pattern in CLAUDE.md

options.label: D
options.text: A user-scoped command for personal use

explanation: Simple slash commands are best for straightforward operations without complex logic or tool requirements. Skills are more appropriate for complex workflows that need structured instructions, tool access, or detailed processing steps.

stem: Your `/code-review` skill has grown from 50 lines to 300 lines as your team added more review criteria. Team members report it's becoming less focused and harder to maintain. What's the best refactoring approach?

options.label: A
options.text: Split into focused skills: `/review-security`, `/review-performance`, `/review-style`

options.label: B
options.text: Move detailed criteria to separate documentation and keep the skill concise

options.label: C
options.text: Create a master skill that delegates to specialized sub-skills

options.label: D
options.text: Convert to multiple slash commands for each review type

explanation: Large skills become unwieldy and less effective. The core skill should remain focused on the review process, with detailed criteria moved to referenced documentation. This maintains usability while preserving comprehensive guidance.

stem: A developer implements a `/continue-refactoring` skill with `context: shared` expecting it to automatically continue from previous refactoring discussions. The skill still asks for context about what needs refactoring. What's the misconception?

options.label: A
options.text: Context: shared doesn't exist; skills always use context: fork

options.label: B
options.text: Context: shared requires explicit conversation history passing

options.label: C
options.text: Skills need context: inherit to access previous conversation

options.label: D
options.text: The skill needs allowed-tools: ['Memory'] to access conversation history

explanation: Skills execute with context: fork (isolation) by design. There is no context: shared option. If continuation is needed, the skill must be designed to accept context as parameters or the conversation should continue without invoking an isolated skill.

key_concept_tested: optimizing skill loading and token usage
stem: Your development team has 20 different skills for various tasks. Developers report that Claude sometimes seems slower and uses more tokens than expected. What's the most likely cause and solution?

options.label: A
options.text: Too many skills are auto-invoking; switch to manual invocation only

options.label: B
options.text: Skills are too large; break them into smaller, focused skills

options.label: C
options.text: Some frequently-used skill content should be moved to CLAUDE.md

options.label: D
options.text: Skills should be consolidated into fewer, comprehensive skills

explanation: If certain skill content is used very frequently, it might be more efficient in CLAUDE.md to avoid repeated loading. The key is identifying which content is used often enough to justify always-loaded context versus on-demand skill loading.

key_concept_tested: slash command vs skill execution model differences
stem: What's the key execution difference between a slash command and a skill when invoked by a user?

options.label: A
options.text: Slash commands run in the main conversation context, skills run in isolated sub-agents

options.label: B
options.text: Slash commands are faster, skills provide more detailed responses

options.label: C
options.text: Slash commands can't access tools, skills can use allowed-tools

options.label: D
options.text: Slash commands are user-scoped only, skills are always project-scoped

stem: In multi-pass document extraction, what is the key principle for determining how much context to carry forward between passes?

explanation: The key principle is maintaining extraction consistency - each pass needs sufficient context from previous passes to make coherent decisions that align with earlier findings. Too little context causes inconsistencies, while too much context can overwhelm the analysis focus of each pass.

stem: A developer implements this validation approach: 'After extraction, the same instance reviews its output and identifies potential issues. For each issue, it re-extracts just that portion with additional attention.' This shows minimal improvement. What's the fundamental problem?

options.label: B
options.text: The same reasoning limitations that caused issues initially persist in re-extraction

options.label: D

explanation: The fundamental problem is that the same instance brings the same reasoning limitations, knowledge gaps, and cognitive biases to the re-extraction process. If it misunderstood a document section initially due to domain knowledge gaps or reasoning blind spots, those same limitations will affect the re-extraction attempt.

stem: Your CI/CD system processes a pull request with 23 files: 8 core business logic, 7 API endpoints, 5 database models, 3 utility functions. For efficient multi-pass review, how should you structure the analysis passes?

stem: When implementing confidence scores for document extraction, what is the most important characteristic for ensuring reliable downstream decision-making?
